points: Clonal endothelial proliferation, **GLUT-1 positive** (unlike malformations and congenital haemangiomas).
Risk factors: prematurity, low birth weight, female sex, multiple pregnancy, placental anomalies.

visuals.caption: Natural history of infantile haemangioma: appearance (0–2 weeks), rapid growth (1–6 months), slow involution, and completion (5–7+ years).

items.name: Deep
items.t: Bluish, rubbery swelling under the skin

points: Ultrasound if deep, or uncertain against a malformation or soft-tissue mass. MRI for complex facial or segmental lesions.
Abdominal ultrasound if there are 5 or more skin lesions.

cards.name: Port-wine stain (see Port-wine stain)
cards.clue: Present at birth, flat, **grows with the child**, no rapid tumour growth

cards.name: Congenital haemangioma
cards.clue: Fully formed at birth; different natural history

cards.name: Pyogenic granuloma
cards.clue: Later onset; often a pedunculated bleeding papule

rungs.k: Refer promptly (ideally by about 4 weeks of age if high risk)
points: Nasal tip, large facial, or **segmental** (PHACE risk with large facial segmental lesions)

Oral **propranolol** is first line for problematic IH. It is started and supervised by a specialist, with heart rate, BP and glucose monitoring. Feed regularly, and **hold doses if the baby is unwell or not feeding**.
Topical **timolol** for selected small, thin, superficial lesions (off-label; NICE ESUOM47).
Wound care, analgesia and antibiotics for ulceration; laser or surgery for selected residual changes.

items.t: High-risk haemangioma sites (listed above): **do not wait to see if it goes away**.
Stridor or noisy breathing with a beard-area haemangioma: **urgent**.

pearls.t: The rapid growth window is early, so **late referral misses the easiest window for treatment**.
IP role: recognise high-risk sites, explain that beta-blockers are specialist-supervised, and support dressings for ulceration under the specialist plan.
BAD patient leaflet and the Birthmark Support Group are useful for families.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: High-risk haemangioma sites (listed above): **do not wait to see if it goes away**.
